description:
Make Any Milk or Cream at Home 

Ever needed 3.5% milk, 10% cream, or 18% cream—and didn’t have it?

In this video, I’ll show you how to accurately convert 33% cream + water into any milk or cream, while maintaining proper texture using skim milk powder where it actually matters. There is also a chart that shows how to do the same with 30% cream, 33%, 36% and 50% creams!

You will only need the cream, cold water and skim milk powder (or substitute). 

⸻
Downloadable chart availabile to Channel members and Patreon Supporters. 

Get the exact gram-based formulas here:
👉 https://www.patreon.com/PolarIceCreamery

⸻

🧑‍🍳 Why This Matters

If you cook, bake, or make ice cream, this gives you full control over your dairy without stocking multiple products. It will also save you money as discussed in the video. 

It’s also a huge upgrade for:
 • Coffee & barista use
 • Sauce and pastry work
 • Ice cream base development

⸻

🔧 Gear I Use
 • Precision scale (grams)
 • High-fat cream (30–50%)
 • Skim milk powder (coconut milk powder, soy milk powder etc also suitable)

⸻

👍 If You Found This Useful

Like, subscribe, and check out the Patreon for more deep-dive food science tools and recipes.

⸻

comments.text:
Love your science based content.
I did some number crunching awhile ago and found that it is substantally cheaper to make the 33% Whipping Cream using whole milk and salt free butter than buying the whipping cream, at least where i live in California. It's not hard to do. Involves heat, which we're doing for the stabilizer, anyway. This way i just need whole milk and butter in stock. You also have more control over things like premium milk, butter, organic, grass fed, etc if you want and still be cheaper than whipping cream. Then, instead of mixing whole milk with whipping cream, just calculate the whole milk portion of the mix, and add the appropriate amount of butter
 butter during the heating stage. I'm guessing the ice cream calculators can probably do most if that work. Would like your thoughts on this.
Second point, my son is lactose intolerant. Since you use so many different milk products (whole, whipping, cream cheese, etc,), they aren't all available in lactose free. I realized that i can deal with the whole problem by treating the entire batch using Milkaid (lactase) drops just before puting it into the frig. If you heated the batch for stabilizers, you have to let it cool down to 131 F before adding the drops so you don't kill the enzymes. Add 10 drops/500 ml of base and put it into the frig for 24hrs for 99% lactose free. That time is based on starting with refrigerated milk. Since we're starting with a warmer base, might be able to shorten that time a little,  or just figure we a built in safety margin.
Thanks again for all your content. I'm only a YouTube member now, but when my time and money frees up a little, I'll probably be joining Patrion at some level.
comments.author: @kkorff
